newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish health service protests over pay, finance.
newsitem.headline: Polish health service protests over pay, finance.

text.p: Polish doctors and nurses went on strike on Friday, offering only emergency care at scores of hospitals nationwide, to back demands for better pay and financing for the creaking health care system.
The one-day action marks an escalation of a long dispute with the ex-communist-led government by health service workers grouped in the pro-opposition Solidarity trade union.

PAP news agency reported that in the Mazowsze region around Warsaw about 60 health service facilities were taking part in some way, while the protest was also biting in the cities of Poznan, Czestochowa, Zielona Gora and elsewhere.

Apart from pay demands, union leaders say they want the service's past debts to be forgiven, paving the way for a genuine rise in spending on health to six percent of Gross Domestic Product from about 4.4 percent last year.
They also want adoption of Solidarity's proposals for a reform of the health insurance system.
The government is to present its 1997 budget to parliament next week and has promised to grant an increase for health, which it hopes will partially satisfy doctors' demands.
But union chiefs say that unless past debts are written off, this will not mean a real increase.

The government's spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska told a news conference on Monday that it was willing to negotiate and hoped the dispute could be settled. She charged that much of Solidarity's rhetoric over health was purely political.
But PAP quoted Stanislaw Grzonowski, head of Solidarity's health service section in Mazowsze, as telling a Friday rally:
"We stick by our demands to the government and we reject allegations that this is a politically-motivated protest."
The union asked people who did not have very pressing problems to stay away from clinics and hospitals for the day.
Doctors have been holding brief one-day strikes at selected hospitals and 10,000 of them staged a silent march through Warsaw a month ago.
They also plan shortly to stop signing sick-leave forms, a move which could give employers and officials in the social security system a serious administrative headache.
